title: Colicky abdominal pain and vomiting in a 58-year-old woman
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 58-year-old woman in the ED with colicky periumbilical pain, worsening vomiting, absolute constipation and a previous laparoscopic operation. The candidate then interprets her observations, bloods, venous gas and CT report, names the diagnosis and differentials, and outlines the initial management, surgical referral and safety netting.
focus: Acute abdominal pain with vomiting: recognising and managing adhesive small bowel obstruction
stem: You are an intern working in a busy metropolitan Emergency Department. Bertha Bartholomew, a 58-year-old primary school teacher, has just come in with severe abdominal pain. She has been put in a bay and your consultant has asked you to see her. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, blood results and venous gas, and a CT report. Hand over and interpret them, give your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bertha Bartholomew, a 58-year-old primary school teacher. You are lying on the trolley in obvious pain with an emesis bag beside you. You shift about and draw your knees up during each wave of pain, then settle between waves. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I have really bad tummy pain and I've been vomiting!"

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • Around the belly button. It does not go anywhere else.
  • "Stabbing" and crampy. It comes in waves and eases off between them.
  • Started yesterday late morning, gradually, not suddenly. It has got worse over the last few hours. You have never had anything like it before.
  • About 7 out of 10 at first, now 8 to 9 out of 10. You cannot do much and slept badly.
  • Nothing in particular makes the pain worse, though pressing on your tummy is sore. Vomiting eases it for a while. Eating or moving doesn't change it; you haven't eaten since yesterday morning.
  • No injury to the tummy.

The vomiting

  • Started yesterday early afternoon, a few hours after the pain.
  • Every 1 to 2 hours, usually when the pain peaks, about half a cup to a cup each time.
  • At first it looked like normal vomit. Now it is brown and smells much worse.
  • No blood in it.

Other symptoms (you give these only to specific questions; if asked vaguely "anything else?", say "I'm not sure, like what?")

  • Nausea since yesterday.
  • One bad episode of diarrhoea yesterday around lunchtime, soon after the pain started. Nothing at all since then: no stool and no wind. You normally go every day.
  • Your tummy feels bloated.
  • Sweaty, and you have lost your appetite.
  • No blood from the back passage. No reflux or trouble swallowing.
  • No yellowing of your skin or eyes. No black or tarry stools.
  • No fever and no weight loss.
  • No chest pain or palpitations. No urinary symptoms now.

Past history

  • High blood pressure.
  • A urinary tract infection last month.
  • One operation on your tummy: keyhole surgery for a burst ovarian cyst at age 30, with no complications. No other operations.
  • No heart rhythm problems, heart disease, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease or diabetes.

Medications and allergies

  • Perindopril 4 mg daily.
  • Only if asked about recent medicines or antibiotics: a 5-day course of amoxicillin with clavulanate for the urine infection, finished 3 weeks ago.
  • No other changes and no laxatives. No known drug allergies.

Family history: your mother has high blood pressure.

Social history

  • You live with your partner. Your two adult children have moved out.
  • Home-cooked meals. You walk with a neighbourhood walking group.
  • Ex-smoker: 20 pack-years, quit at 45.
  • One glass of red wine a day.
  • No recent travel, no recent illness and nobody unwell around you.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "No idea, maybe I ate something bad?" You are frightened because the pain is the worst you have had. You want something for the pain and the vomiting and want to know what is going on.

The nurse and how Bertha changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the ones listed under Exam findings.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "She has just vomited again, about a cup of brown, foul-smelling fluid."
  • If the candidate gives or orders IV analgesia, Bertha's pain eases to about 5 out of 10 a few minutes later and she answers more easily. If not, she stays at 8 to 9 out of 10.
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic or a nasogastric tube, the nurse confirms she will arrange it.
  • If the candidate asks for bloods, a gas or imaging in Part 1, the examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (examiner gives each only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • Observations: HR 110 regular, BP 128/78, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C, BGL 6.4 mmol/L.
  • General: unwell, pale and in obvious pain. Bilious and faeculent material in the emesis bag beside the bed.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes. CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
  • Hands, face and neck: no stigmata of chronic liver disease. No supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Abdomen, inspection: obviously distended. Three small, well-healed laparoscopic scars (umbilical, right iliac fossa, left iliac fossa).
  • Hernial orifices: no hernias at the inguinal, femoral or umbilical regions or the port sites. Cough impulse negative.
  • Palpation: tender throughout. No masses. No guarding, rigidity or rebound tenderness.
  • Percussion: tympanic.
  • Auscultation: tinkling bowel sounds.
  • PR: empty rectum. No blood, no mass.
  • Heart and lungs: normal.
  • Everything else normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms the patient's identity, acknowledges her pain and offers or arranges analgesia and an antiemetic early, without waiting until the end of the history.
Uses plain language and empathy with a distressed patient, explains each part of the examination before doing it, and keeps the history focused.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: periumbilical, no radiation
Onset and course: started yesterday late morning, gradual, comes and goes, worse in the last few hours, never had it before
Character and severity: stabbing and crampy (colicky), 8 to 9 out of 10
Modifying factors: eased by vomiting, no relation to food or movement

check.x: Characterises the vomiting: elicits the change to brown, foul-smelling (faeculent) vomit and asks specifically about blood, plus at least 2 of onset (yesterday early afternoon), frequency (every 1 to 2 hours with the pain peaks) and volume (half a cup to a cup).
Asks specifically about bowel habit and elicits absolute constipation: no stool or flatus since a single episode of diarrhoea yesterday lunchtime (normally daily), bloating; no blood PR.
Screens at least 4 of: nausea, appetite, reflux, dysphagia, weight loss, haematemesis or melaena, jaundice; and at least 2 of: fever or sweats, chest pain or palpitations, urinary symptoms.
Asks about previous abdominal surgery and elicits the laparoscopic operation for a ruptured ovarian cyst at 30.
Asks about risk factors for the important differentials, at least 4 of: arrhythmia, vascular disease, vasculitis, smoking, IBD, recent antibiotics, trauma, travel or sick contacts.
Takes a medication and allergy history: perindopril 4 mg daily, no laxatives or other recent changes, no known drug allergies.
Takes the past, family and social history: hypertension, UTI last month, mother with hypertension, lives with partner, ex-smoker of 20 pack-years who quit at 45, one glass of wine daily.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including her belief that she ate something bad.
Examination
General inspection: unwell, pale, in pain, and looks in the emesis bag (bilious and faeculent content).
Asks for the vital signs and assesses hydration: HR 110, dry mucous membranes, CRT and peripheral perfusion.
Inspects the abdomen: distension and the three laparoscopic scars.
Examines the hernial orifices (inguinal, femoral, umbilical and port-site scars) with a cough impulse.
Palpates gently for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound and masses, looking for peritonism.
Percusses and auscultates the abdomen (tinkling bowel sounds).
Asks for a PR examination (empty rectum, no blood or mass) and checks for supraclavicular lymph nodes.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: tachycardia rising from 110 to 116 with ongoing vomiting and no urine output means significant fluid loss despite all values being in the white zone.
Identifies a prerenal AKI (creatinine 108 against a baseline of 68, KDIGO stage 1; urea 12.4 disproportionately raised) with hypokalaemia and haemoconcentration from vomiting and third-space losses.
Interprets the venous gas as a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, and states that a normal lactate does not exclude bowel ischaemia.
Interprets the mildly raised WCC and CRP as non-specific and a reason to keep watching for ischaemia.

Interprets the CT: dilated small bowel with a transition point in the right lower quadrant and collapsed distal ileum and colon, no mass or hernia, so most likely an adhesion. Notes that there are no features of ischaemia, closed loop or perforation.

Gives the diagnosis as small bowel obstruction from adhesions after previous abdominal surgery, justified by at least 3 of colicky pain, faeculent vomiting, absolute constipation, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, the previous laparoscopy, and the CT transition point with no mass or hernia.

Gives at least 2 reasonable differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case (for example mesenteric ischaemia: ex-smoker, early diarrhoea, but normal lactate and bowel enhancement; C. difficile colitis or toxic megacolon: recent amoxicillin with clavulanate, but a single episode of diarrhoea and a collapsed colon; large bowel obstruction: collapsed colon on CT; obstructing malignancy: age and smoking, but no mass on CT).
Management

Nil by mouth, IV access, an IV isotonic crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL; 0.9% sodium chloride preferred because it corrects her hypochloraemic alkalosis) with reassessment, then replacement fluid covering ongoing and NG losses.

Replaces potassium for K 3.2 with a premixed potassium-containing bag (e.g. 0.9% sodium chloride with 30 mmol KCl per litre, no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally) once urine output is confirmed, with an IDC and fluid balance chart (target ≥0.5 mL/kg/h, about 35 mL/h); withholds perindopril.
Inserts a nasogastric tube on free drainage with regular aspiration to decompress the stomach.
Gives titrated IV opioid analgesia and a non-prokinetic antiemetic (for example ondansetron), and avoids metoclopramide in mechanical obstruction.
Refers early to general surgery for admission and gives the indications for urgent surgery: ischaemia, peritonitis, closed loop, or failure to settle with non-operative management.
Safety netting

Sets escalation triggers for the nurses and the surgical team (urgent surgical review, or a rapid response if any observation enters the red zone): at least 4 of a rising heart rate, falling BP, fever, pain that becomes constant or out of proportion, new guarding or rigidity, a rising lactate, falling urine output, including a change in the pain or peritonism.

Explains to Bertha in plain words at least 3 of: the bowel is blocked, probably by scar tissue from her old operation and not by something she ate; a tube in the nose and a drip often settle it; she may need an operation; tell the nurse at once if the pain gets worse or constant, or she feels hot or faint.

part2.lead: Here are Bertha's observations, her blood results and venous blood gas, and the CT report.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains to her what is happening (the fourth question), Bertha asks:

  • "So it wasn't something I ate?"
  • "Will I need an operation?"

She is relieved to hear it often settles without surgery but anxious about the tube in her nose. If the candidate uses jargon such as "adhesions" or "NG tube", ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. No urine passed since arrival.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 11:20 pain score is left blank on the chart. If analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate the 11:20 pain score is 5 and IV analgesia has been given. Otherwise, tell them the pain score is 8 and no analgesia has been given.
  • Read: at 10:20, HR 110, BP 128/78, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 37.2 °C are all in the white zone. At 11:20 HR has risen to 116 (still white) and the temperature is 37.4 °C. She has vomited again and has not passed urine. Pain at 11:20 (given by the examiner) is 8 out of 10 without analgesia, or 5 out of 10 if IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1.
  • Meaning: a persistent, slowly rising tachycardia with ongoing vomiting and no urine output points to significant fluid loss (vomiting and third-spacing into the bowel). No value triggers a chart call, but a white zone chart does not mean she is safe. She is afebrile, which is reassuring but does not exclude ischaemia.
  • Changes: needs fluid resuscitation, analgesia (or further titrated doses if already given) and hourly observations with a fluid balance chart. Escalate for a clinical review if any value enters the yellow zone and call a rapid response if any enters the red zone. A rising HR, fever or a change in the pain calls for urgent surgical review.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: very severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardic
Vomited about 300 mL brown, foul-smelling fluid; no urine passed. Pain score: see examiner.

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.model:
• Read: creatinine 108 against a baseline of 68 with urea 12.4: AKI (KDIGO stage 1), with urea raised out of proportion to creatinine, a prerenal pattern. Na 133, K 3.2 and Cl 92 are low. Hb 152 against a baseline of 132 shows haemoconcentration. The venous gas shows pH 7.47 with HCO3 32 and BE +7, a metabolic alkalosis with appropriate pCO2. Lactate 1.4 is normal. WCC 12.6 with neutrophilia and CRP 24 are mildly raised. Lipase, LFTs, INR and glucose are normal.
  • Meaning: dehydration from vomiting and third-space losses causes a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. The mild inflammatory rise is non-specific. A normal lactate is reassuring but does not exclude ischaemia, because lactate rises late. Normal lipase and LFTs make pancreatitis and biliary causes unlikely.
  • Changes: IV 0.9% sodium chloride, which also corrects the chloride-responsive alkalosis, with potassium for K 3.2 as a premixed bag (e.g. 30 mmol KCl per litre, no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally) once urine output is confirmed, with an IDC and fluid balance chart (target ≥0.5 mL/kg/h, about 35 mL/h); repeat UEC; withhold perindopril and avoid nephrotoxins; repeat the lactate if her clinical state changes; group and hold is done in case she needs theatre.

handover.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
handover.result:
Examination: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (portal venous phase). No oral contrast.

Clinical details: 58-year-old woman. Colicky periumbilical pain since yesterday, faeculent vomiting, no flatus or stool since yesterday lunchtime (about 24 hours), distended abdomen with tinkling bowel sounds. Previous laparoscopy for ruptured ovarian cyst. AKI (creatinine 108). ?Bowel obstruction.

Findings:

  • Small bowel: multiple dilated, fluid-filled loops of jejunum and proximal ileum up to 4.2 cm in diameter with air-fluid levels. Particulate material (small bowel faeces sign) in the dilated ileum just proximal to an abrupt transition point in the right lower quadrant, beneath the right iliac fossa port site. Distal ileum beyond the transition point is collapsed. No mass or bowel wall thickening at the transition point.
  • Bowel wall and mesentery: normal enhancement of the small bowel wall. No pneumatosis. No mesenteric swirl, no mesenteric oedema and no closed-loop configuration.
  • Large bowel: collapsed throughout, with little gas or faeces. No colonic dilatation or wall thickening.
  • Peritoneum: small volume of free fluid between the dilated loops. No free intraperitoneal gas. No portal venous gas.
  • Hernial orifices: no inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional or port-site hernia.
  • Vessels: superior mesenteric artery and vein patent with mild atherosclerotic calcification of the aorta.
  • Solid organs: liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, adrenal glands and kidneys normal. No gallstones. No hydronephrosis.
  • Pelvis: uterus and adnexa unremarkable. Bladder decompressed.
  • Lung bases and bones: clear lung bases. No aggressive bony lesion.

Conclusion: high-grade distal small bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right lower quadrant. No mass or hernia, so most likely adhesional. No CT features of ischaemia, closed-loop obstruction or perforation.
handover.model:
• Read: dilated, fluid-filled small bowel up to 4.2 cm (above the usual 3 cm) with a small bowel faeces sign, an abrupt transition point in the right lower quadrant under the old port site, and collapsed distal ileum and colon. No mass, no hernia, normal wall enhancement, no pneumatosis, portal venous gas, free gas, swirl or closed loop. Small volume of free fluid.
  • Meaning: high-grade distal small bowel obstruction from an adhesion related to her previous laparoscopy. This matches the colicky pain, faeculent vomiting, absolute constipation and distension. A collapsed colon argues against large bowel obstruction and toxic megacolon. No hernia or mass makes those causes unlikely. There is currently no CT evidence of strangulation. A small volume of free fluid is common in SBO; a larger or increasing volume, especially with mesenteric oedema, raises concern for strangulation.
  • Changes: admit under general surgery for a trial of non-operative management (nil by mouth, NG decompression, IV fluids, water-soluble contrast with a follow-up X-ray). Surgery is needed if ischaemia or peritonitis develops or the obstruction does not resolve.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bertha Bartholomew, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Bertha now, here in the emergency department.
What would make you escalate, and what will you tell Bertha?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Bertha Bartholomew, 58.
  • Situation: small bowel obstruction, most likely adhesional, with dehydration and AKI; no features of ischaemia so far.
  • Background: colicky periumbilical pain and vomiting since yesterday, now faeculent; no flatus or stool for 24 h; distended, tinkling bowel sounds, no hernia, no peritonism; laparoscopy at 30; on perindopril.
  • Assessment: HR 110 rising to 116, no urine; prerenal AKI (creatinine 108, baseline 68); K 3.2, metabolic alkalosis; lactate 1.4 normal but does not exclude ischaemia; WCC 12.6 and CRP 24 mildly raised, non-specific; CT adhesive SBO, RLQ transition point, no ischaemia or closed loop.
  • Recommendation: NBM, NG tube, IV fluid resuscitation started or requested; please review for admission and non-operative management.

Adhesive small bowel obstruction: colicky pain, faeculent vomiting, absolute constipation, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, laparoscopic scars, and a CT transition point with no mass or hernia.

  • Mesenteric ischaemia (must not miss): ex-smoker, early diarrhoea; against: normal lactate, normal bowel enhancement.
  • C. difficile colitis or toxic megacolon: recent amoxicillin with clavulanate; against: one episode of diarrhoea, collapsed colon.
  • Large bowel obstruction: against: collapsed colon on CT.
  • Obstructing malignancy: age, smoking; against: no mass on CT.

1. Nil by mouth, IV access, bloods already sent (group and hold).
  2. IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (e.g. 500 mL), reassess, then replacement for ongoing and NG losses; potassium as a premixed bag (e.g. 30 mmol KCl/L, ≤10 mmol/h peripherally) once she is passing urine.
  3. IDC and fluid balance chart (≥0.5 mL/kg/h); withhold perindopril.
  4. NG tube on free drainage with regular aspiration.
  5. Titrated IV opioid; ondansetron, not metoclopramide.
  6. Early general surgical referral for admission; surgery for ischaemia, peritonitis, closed loop or failure to settle.

• Escalate (urgent surgical review, or rapid response if in the red zone) for rising HR, falling BP, fever, constant or worsening pain, peritonism, rising lactate, falling urine output.
  • Explain to Bertha: a blockage in the bowel, probably from scar tissue from her old operation, not something she ate; a tube in the nose empties the stomach and a drip replaces fluid; it often settles without an operation but she may need one, and it can recur.
  • Tell the nurse at once about worse or constant pain, feeling hot or feeling faint.

guide:
In Part 1, Bertha answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. She gives the associated symptoms only to specific questions. If asked a vague "anything else?", she says "I'm not sure, like what?". The nurse reports the second episode of faeculent vomiting partway through. If the candidate asks for investigations in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, and the CT report, then ask all four questions in order. The 11:20 pain score is blank on the chart: if analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate the pain score is 5 and IV analgesia has been given; otherwise tell them it is 8 and no analgesia has been given. Bertha's questions are put while the candidate answers the fourth question (what they will tell her).

A high-performing candidate takes a full history of both the pain and the vomiting and asks specifically about bowel motions and flatus. They elicit the previous laparoscopy, screen the risk factors for ischaemia and colitis (including the recent amoxicillin with clavulanate), and offer analgesia early. They examine the hydration, scars, hernial orifices (including femoral) and the abdomen for peritonism, and ask for a PR. In Part 2 they recognise a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, state that a normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia, and read the CT as adhesive small bowel obstruction without strangulation. They resuscitate, decompress with an NG tube, avoid metoclopramide, refer to general surgery, know when surgery is needed and set clear escalation triggers.

A borderline candidate takes the pain history but does not ask about flatus or previous surgery, and omits the hernial orifices or the PR. They may call the gas "normal" or be reassured by the lactate, and may treat the vomiting with metoclopramide or plan oral fluids. Their management may stop at "surgical review" without fluids, NG decompression or escalation triggers.
explain:
Diagnosis: adhesive small bowel obstruction

Bertha has the four cardinal features of bowel obstruction: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and absolute constipation (no stool and no flatus). The vomiting has turned faeculent, which points to a distal (ileal) level, as does the marked distension. Her only risk factor is a previous laparoscopy, but even one abdominal or pelvic operation is enough to form adhesions. Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults. The single episode of diarrhoea soon after the pain began is common in SBO, as the bowel beyond the obstruction empties.

Small bowel obstruction varies with its timing, level and whether it is strangulated. Proximal obstruction gives early, marked vomiting with little distension. Distal obstruction gives more distension, colic with longer intervals, and later, often faeculent vomiting. Strangulation (compromised blood supply, often in a closed loop or hernia) turns colicky pain constant, with fever, tachycardia, peritonism and a rising lactate and WCC, and is a surgical emergency.

History and examination

Use reading time to list the causes of severe abdominal pain at this age and let them guide the questions. Take a full history of both the pain and the vomiting, and ask specifically about bowel habit and flatus, because patients rarely volunteer these. Screen for the important differentials:

  • Ischaemia: arrhythmia, vascular disease, vasculitis, smoking.
  • Colitis and toxic megacolon: IBD, recent antibiotics.
  • Malignancy: weight loss, change in bowel habit.

On examination, assess hydration, inspect for scars and distension, examine every hernial orifice (a small femoral hernia in a woman is easily missed), and palpate for peritonism. A PR examination and a look for supraclavicular nodes complete the screen for malignancy.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: a rising tachycardia with no urine output means significant fluid loss, even though all values are in the white zone. Repeat them hourly.
  • Renal function and electrolytes: vomiting and third-space losses into the bowel and peritoneum cause a prerenal AKI (urea rising more than creatinine) and haemoconcentration. Loss of gastric acid and chloride, with aldosterone driving potassium loss, gives a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Lactate: it rises late in ischaemia, so a normal lactate does not exclude strangulation. Clinical reassessment matters more.
  • CT with IV contrast: the investigation of choice. It confirms the obstruction, finds the transition point and the cause (here no mass or hernia, so adhesional), and looks for ischaemia: reduced wall enhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas, mesenteric oedema or swirl, a closed loop, or free gas.

Differentials

  • Mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion to the signs, in smokers and in patients with AF or vascular disease. Bloody diarrhoea may come later.
  • Toxic megacolon: from C. difficile colitis after antibiotics (Bertha had amoxicillin with clavulanate) or IBD. It gives diarrhoea, fever and a dilated colon. Her CT shows a collapsed colon.
  • Large bowel obstruction: often from malignancy or volvulus. It causes earlier constipation and distension with later vomiting, and a dilated colon on imaging.
  • Malignancy: can obstruct the small bowel directly or through peritoneal disease.

Common causes of small bowel obstruction in adults

Adhesions (most common), hernias, malignancy and Crohn's disease, followed by appendicitis and other inflammatory masses, gallstone ileus, volvulus, intussusception and radiation strictures.

Management

Initial ("drip and suck"):

  • Nil by mouth.
  • IV 0.9% sodium chloride to resuscitate: its chloride corrects the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis of vomiting, which a balanced solution (whose lactate or acetate becomes bicarbonate) corrects less well. Then replacement fluid covering ongoing and NG losses, with potassium for K 3.2 as a commercially premixed bag (no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally); concentrated potassium ampoules are not added to bags on the ward.
  • NG tube on free drainage with regular aspiration.
  • An IDC with a fluid balance chart (urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h) before and during potassium replacement; repeat UEC.
  • Titrated IV opioid analgesia.
  • An antiemetic that is not prokinetic. Metoclopramide is avoided in mechanical obstruction.
  • Withhold perindopril during the AKI.
  • VTE prophylaxis agreed with the surgical team.
  • Antibiotics are not routine and are given only if ischaemia, perforation or peritonitis is suspected.

Definitive: the WSES (Bologna) guidelines recommend non-operative management for adhesive SBO without signs of strangulation or peritonitis. A water-soluble contrast agent (such as Gastrografin), given orally or via the NG tube, is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Contrast reaching the colon on a follow-up abdominal X-ray within 24 hours predicts resolution. Give water-soluble contrast after initial resuscitation (it is hyperosmolar and can draw fluid into the bowel). A stage 1 AKI should not delay contrast CT when obstruction or ischaemia is suspected. Failure to progress, or no resolution after about 72 hours of non-operative management, is an indication for surgery. Peritonitis, strangulation, a closed loop or CT signs of ischaemia need urgent surgery.

Safety netting

Nurses escalate for a rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, fever, pain that becomes constant or out of proportion, new guarding, a rising lactate or falling urine output. These may mean strangulation. Bertha should tell staff at once about worse or constant pain, fever or feeling faint. Adhesive obstruction can recur. After discharge she returns to ED for crampy pain, vomiting, bloating or not passing wind, and sees her GP to recheck renal function before restarting perindopril.
points: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus) are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous surgery.
Adhesions from previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, even one laparoscopy, are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults. Hernias, malignancy and Crohn's disease follow.
Proximal small bowel obstruction gives early, marked vomiting with little distension. Distal obstruction gives more distension, colic with longer intervals, and later, often faeculent vomiting.
Vomiting and third-space losses cause a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. A normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia.
Manage with nil by mouth, IV fluids with potassium, NG decompression, analgesia and a non-prokinetic antiemetic (avoid metoclopramide), and early general surgical referral.
Adhesive SBO without strangulation is managed non-operatively with water-soluble contrast. Peritonitis, ischaemia, a closed loop or failure to resolve need surgery.

ddx.against: Lactate is normal, bowel wall enhancement is normal, the SMA and SMV are patent, she has no AF and the pain is colicky, not constant.

ddx.dx: Clostridioides difficile colitis with toxic megacolon
ddx.for: She finished amoxicillin with clavulanate 3 weeks ago and had an episode of diarrhoea when the pain started.
ddx.against: She had only one episode of diarrhoea and nothing since, she is afebrile, and the colon is collapsed on CT with no wall thickening.

ddx.for: She has marked distension, absolute constipation and faeculent vomiting.
ddx.against: Vomiting began within hours of the pain, and CT shows a collapsed colon with the transition point in the small bowel.

ddx.dx: Obstructing malignancy (small bowel tumour or peritoneal disease)
ddx.for: She is 58 and an ex-smoker of 20 pack-years.
ddx.against: There is no mass or wall thickening at the transition point, no weight loss or change in bowel habit before this, no blood PR, and no supraclavicular nodes.
